overview.text: Turbulence is an irregular way that a fluid—a liquid or a gas—moves, unlike the smoother, layered motion of laminar flow. In turbulent flow, swirling structures called eddies appear at many sizes, and local velocities fluctuate around an average. These motions carry fluid across the main direction of flow, mixing and spreading dye, heat, or other materials more effectively than laminar motion. Turbulence matters in rivers, pipes, and air moving near objects because it changes momentum transfer and forces on surfaces. The Reynolds number compares inertia with viscosity; larger values favor turbulence, but there is no universal cutoff: boundaries and flow conditions can shift when turbulent motion begins.

key_facts.text: The Reynolds number compares a flow’s inertia with its viscosity. A higher value favors turbulent motion, but the transition depends on conditions such as boundary roughness and how the flow enters.
Turbulent flow combines a mean flow with fluctuating motion; eddies of different sizes can carry fluid across the main flow’s streamlines.
Eddies can spread dye and transport heat, momentum, and other material through a fluid, making turbulence important to mixing and flow behavior.
In an energy cascade, energy passes mostly from larger eddies to smaller ones; viscosity dampens velocity fluctuations at the smallest scales.
Near an object, its boundary layer can be laminar or turbulent; turbulent boundary layers contain unsteady swirling motion and affect aerodynamic forces such as drag and lift.
